title: AI in Legal Education
description: Law schools now teach AI literacy alongside doctrine: courses on AI and the law cover algorithmic liability, evidence from machine systems, and the unauthorized-practice questions raised by legal chatbots. Bar examiners are studying how AI assistance changes what competence means.
content:
Law schools now teach AI literacy alongside doctrine: courses on AI and the law cover algorithmic liability, evidence from machine systems, and the unauthorized-practice questions raised by legal chatbots. Bar examiners are studying how AI assistance changes what competence means.

The public debate is substantive: AI can draft, research, and summarize, but accountability still attaches to the licensed attorney. Schools respond with disclosure rules and AI-use policies rather than bans.

The durable lesson is that professions absorb tools by redefining supervision, not by pretending the tools do not exist.

Good pedagogy pairs AI with verification: the student proposes, the AI critiques, the student checks the AI against primary sources. Assessment is moving toward process, showing the reasoning, over product.

The evidence base is young but the direction is clear: AI as Socratic partner beats AI as answer machine.

Personalization's frontier is not more content but better diagnosis of what the student actually misunderstands.

title: Collective Intelligence Systems
description: Collective intelligence aggregates many minds, human or artificial, into decisions better than any member's: prediction markets, Delphi panels, and ensemble models all exploit the same mathematics of error cancellation.
content:
Collective intelligence aggregates many minds, human or artificial, into decisions better than any member's: prediction markets, Delphi panels, and ensemble models all exploit the same mathematics of error cancellation.

The conditions matter: independence, diversity, and good aggregation rules. Correlated errors destroy the benefit, which is why ensemble diversity is engineered, not assumed.

Human-AI collectives are the current frontier: people plus models voting, debating, and checking each other.

t: Expert Systems: The First AI Representatives
title: Expert Systems: The First AI Representatives
description: The 1980s expert systems, MYCIN for medicine, XCON for configuring computers, encoded human expertise as rules and explained their reasoning. They were the first AI representatives: software standing in for specialists.
content:
The 1980s expert systems, MYCIN for medicine, XCON for configuring computers, encoded human expertise as rules and explained their reasoning. They were the first AI representatives: software standing in for specialists.

They failed on brittleness: rules covered the known cases and broke on the unknown, and maintaining the knowledge base cost more than building it. Machine learning's statistical approach replaced them.

Their legacy is the explanation requirement: modern AI is still judged by the standard MYCIN set, show your work.
key_facts: MYCIN, XCON: rules encoding specialist expertise
Brittleness: broke on unknown cases; costly maintenance
Replaced by statistical machine learning
Legacy: the explanation requirement

title: AI Agents as Representatives
description: Modern AI agents act as representatives: booking, coding, researching, and negotiating within delegated authority. The architecture is perception, planning, tool use, and memory, looped until the task completes.
content:
Modern AI agents act as representatives: booking, coding, researching, and negotiating within delegated authority. The architecture is perception, planning, tool use, and memory, looped until the task completes.

The hard problems are reliability and scope: agents that work in demos fail on edge cases, and authority without oversight invites misuse. Guardrails, audit logs, and human approval gates are the current answer.

Representation is delegation, and delegation's rules, from power of attorney to API scopes, are the right mental model.
key_facts: Perception, planning, tool use, memory, looped
Hard problems: reliability, scope, oversight
Guardrails, audit logs, approval gates
Delegation law is the right mental model

title: Keeping Knowledge Current
description: A knowledge system's value decays with staleness: RAG indexes, fine-tune schedules, and continuous evaluation exist to fight it. The engineering question is update cadence versus cost, and the answer differs by domain.
content:
A knowledge system's value decays with staleness: RAG indexes, fine-tune schedules, and continuous evaluation exist to fight it. The engineering question is update cadence versus cost, and the answer differs by domain.

Medical and legal knowledge changes fastest and matters most; the systems serving those fields version aggressively and cite sources. Provenance, knowing where each fact came from, is what makes updates trustworthy.

Current beats large: a smaller current model outperforms a larger stale one on time-sensitive questions.

Medicine and law change fastest, version aggressively
Provenance makes updates trustworthy
Current beats large on time-sensitive questions

title: Ethics of AI in Education
description: The ethical questions are concrete: surveillance versus support in proctoring, equity when AI access is uneven, and the deskilling risk when students never struggle. Each has public debate and emerging norms.
content:
The ethical questions are concrete: surveillance versus support in proctoring, equity when AI access is uneven, and the deskilling risk when students never struggle. Each has public debate and emerging norms.

The consensus forming is human-centered: AI should increase student agency, not replace it, and institutions owe transparency about where AI decides. Opt-outs and audits are the mechanisms.

Ethics here is applied, not abstract: policies, not principles, are what protect students.

title: The Future University
description: The plausible future university is hybrid: physical for community and labs, digital for content and practice, AI for tutoring at scale. Credentials unbundle into verifiable skills; the degree becomes a portfolio.
content:
The plausible future university is hybrid: physical for community and labs, digital for content and practice, AI for tutoring at scale. Credentials unbundle into verifiable skills; the degree becomes a portfolio.

The functions that survive are mentorship, certification, and community, the things scale cannot replace. Content delivery, already commoditized, finishes its migration to machines.

Institutions that embrace the unbundling will define it; those that resist will watch it happen anyway.
